Those two can sometimes coexist, but as a three-item profile with shame on recall they pull in opposing directions and are clinically questionable together.

The threat and memory items center on being followed, danger in unfamiliar places, delays, shame, and vivid reliving; enclosed spaces introduces a more specific situational avoidance that is not supported by the memory/threat content and looks disconnected from the formulation, especially since Triggers is not active in this case.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits in tension with 'When I remember the event I feel intense shame' and 'Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time.' Severe shame and terror on recall usually make disclosure difficult rather than easy, so this combination is clinically questionable within the same node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: 'Ruminate about how to get even with assailant' is a poor fit with the rest of the profile for this trauma type and patient presentation. The Memory and Threat items emphasize shame, terror, hypervigilance, and avoidance, which is more consistent with fear-based post-assault PTSD; revenge-focused rumination pulls toward a different emotional/cognitive stance and lacks support elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: 'Gambling' is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly anchored to the rest of the presentation. The dominant active formulation is Memory↔Threat↔Maladaptive Strategies around trauma recollection and danger monitoring after sexual assault; gambling for excitement/distracting oneself is too nonspecific and does not connect clearly to the patient's other selected threat and memory items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Enclosed Spaces' appears to be a trigger/avoidance cue rather than a maladaptive strategy, and it is poorly matched to the rest of the profile. The threat and memory items center on being followed, danger in unfamiliar places, shame, terror, and speechless recall; avoidance of enclosed spaces is a different contextual pattern that is not otherwise supported here.

vignette:
David was a 53-year-old social worker who had spent two decades at a community mental health center, dedicated to helping clients navigate their own darkest moments. The sexual assault happened in a windowless storage room adjacent to his office, a small space he had used to store intake files. A client he had been trying to stabilize for months cornered him there after a session, and in that confined, windowless space, the attack became something David could not name aloud, even to himself. The memory came back not as a coherent narrative he could tell his wife or his supervisor, but as a sudden, suffocating wave of raw terror and a crushing sense of shame that left him breathless. In the weeks that followed, he tried to push the whole thing out of his mind, telling himself to just get back to work, that it was part of the job, that he should be able to handle it. But the physical memory of being sexually violated-the feeling of helplessness, the invasiveness of it-lodged itself in his body, surfacing as a queasy, hot flash whenever he thought about that room or that client.

Work became a minefield. The storage room was sealed shut and never used again, but every closed door at the agency now made his chest tighten-especially doors leading to small, windowless spaces like the copy room or the staff restroom. He started taking the stairs instead of the elevator, arriving at third-floor meetings drenched in sweat and lightheaded, because riding in that enclosed metal box felt too much like being trapped. He began turning down home visits to unfamiliar neighborhoods, offering thin excuses to his supervisor about scheduling conflicts that he could not quite justify to her or to himself. The hypervigilance was exhausting and inescapable. He found himself constantly looking over his shoulder, scanning parking lots and office corridors for any male client who seemed agitated or too familiar. If a colleague was five minutes late for a supervision meeting, his mind would instantly race to the worst possible conclusion-that he was about to be cornered again, that he would be sexually assaulted again. He had come to believe that the world was neatly divided into safe, known spaces and dangerous, unknown ones, and the territory of the safe ones was steadily shrinking.

At home, a different kind of torture consumed him. He spent hours replaying the assault, not to process what had happened, but to mentally plot a revenge he knew he would never actually take. He would imagine confronting his assailant in vivid detail-pinning him down, making him feel the same degradation-and these fantasies left him feeling agitated and morally sickened, yet he could not stop the loop from running. The shame of having been sexually assaulted by a client, a man he had been trying to help, was layered with shame about his own vengeful thoughts. His wife noticed the distance growing between them. He was irritable and withdrawn, staring at the wall during dinner, unable to explain the storm inside him. When she asked what was wrong, he would say "nothing" and force the thoughts down again, a strategy that only deepened his shame and isolation, because he knew the "nothing" was a lie.

By the time David walked into the clinic, what finally brought him in was a quiet ultimatum from his wife, coupled with a formal complaint from his agency director about his declining availability for field visits. He was terrified of being seen as broken or weak-a man who could not protect himself, a social worker who could no longer do the job he had spent his life building. He was also terrified of the specific shame of admitting that what had happened to him was a sexual assault, that he had been sexually violated in a way that he had always associated with vulnerability and femininity. But he was also terrified of staying the same. More than anything, David hoped to find a way to live without the constant vigilance that made his own office feel like a trap, without the shame that made him want to disappear every time the memory of that room and that helplessness surfaced, and without the anger that was slowly poisoning everything he had worked for. He hoped, somehow, to finally find the words.
